fixes.name: Random (compulsory) breath testing at high volume, Australian, New Zealand and Nordic model
fixes.how_it_works: Police stop drivers at random, with no suspicion needed, and breath-test every one, at a rate high enough that most drivers expect to be tested each year.

groups.mechanism: Drivers expect to be tested on any trip, so fewer drive after drinking at all; US checkpoints test only drivers who show signs.
groups.target_share: Group total 851 hurt / 68 KSI people (size_families.chart); the whole group is alcohol-involved by definition

effect.unit: % change in crashes (low and mid: all checkpoint crashes, meta-analysis; high: NSW fatal crashes, multi-year average)
effect.applies_to: Low and mid: Erke, Goldenbeld and Vaa 2009 meta-analysis of DUI checkpoints, crashes -17% overall, -14% after correcting for publication bias, alcohol-involved crashes at least -17%; it pooled random and selective testing. High: NSW after RBT began in December 1982, fatal crashes about -22% over five years against five before (an initial drop of 48% lasted two to four months); alcohol-related fatal and serious crashes -35%
effect.source: Erke et al. 2009, Accident Analysis and Prevention 41(5) (abstract via search); Homel, Henstridge and McKay, NSW RBT time series (via search and UK Hansard 1989)

groups.mechanism: Same deterrence for drivers who later hit someone walking.
groups.target_share: Group total 94 hurt / 30 KSI people (size_families.chart); the party coded DUI may be the pedestrian, whom RBT does not reach; split not computed

effect.unit: % change in crashes
effect.applies_to: As for vehicles only | DUI
effect.source: Erke et al. 2009; Homel et al.

groups.mechanism: Most RBT effect lands in night-time single-vehicle crashes, where drinking concentrates.
groups.target_share: 2,974 hurt / 240 KSI people, vehicles only, weekday plus weekend late night (grouping_alternatives). Alcohol share basis: among KSI people whose at-fault driver's sobriety was recorded, the driver had been drinking in 28 of 54 late-night cases (52%) and 31 of 274 at other hours (11%) (2026-11-20-dui-cost-effective.md)

effect.unit: % change in alcohol-involved crashes; apply only to the drinking share
effect.applies_to: As above; the Australian federal study found the clearest effect on single-vehicle night-time crashes
effect.source: Australian federal report CR 162 (1997), via search

cost.unit: per test or per year: not found. A California program would need a state law first, so there is no SF price; Australian programs run several million tests a year (NSW) [model knowledge — verify]

fixes.sf_now: California allows sobriety checkpoints under Ingersoll v. Palmer (1987) guidelines, which require stops to follow a neutral formula and be publicized; SF ran a handful a year in 2025 (DUI note). Suspicionless testing of every stopped driver at RBT volume is not done.
fixes.who_decides: California Legislature and courts (Fourth Amendment and state constitution limits); SFPD and CHP run operations.
fixes.evidence_grade: moderate: a large meta-analysis and long time series from several Australian states agree on direction; the US legal setting is different and no US city has run it.

sources.title: Erke, Goldenbeld and Vaa 2009, The effects of drink-driving checkpoints on crashes, a meta-analysis
Australian Government, Long-term effects of random breath testing in four Australian states (CR 162, 1997)
UK Hansard, Random breath testing, 4 April 1989 (NSW figures)

fixes.name: 24/7 Sobriety program for people arrested or convicted for DUI (South Dakota model)
fixes.how_it_works: People charged with or convicted of DUI must take a breath test twice a day or wear an alcohol-monitoring bracelet, and any failed or missed test brings a swift, short jail stay.

groups.mechanism: Repeat drink-drivers are kept sober day to day, so they stop re-offending while enrolled.
groups.target_share: Group total 851 hurt / 68 KSI people (size_families.chart); the program reaches only crashes by people with a prior DUI arrest, a share not in results.json

effect.unit: % change (high: repeat DUI arrests at county level; low: all-driver traffic crashes)
effect.applies_to: High: repeat DUI arrests IRR 0.883 (P = .023), a 12% cut; domestic violence arrests -9.5%. Low: traffic crashes, all drivers, IRR 0.980 (P = .338), not significant; men 18 to 40, IRR 0.956 (P = .085). Mid set between the two [inference — mine]. A later study (Nicosia, Kilmer and Heaton) reported lower all-cause mortality [model knowledge — verify]
effect.source: Kilmer et al. 2013, AJPH 103(1), Table 2

groups.mechanism: Same, for drivers who would re-offend and hit someone walking.

effect.unit: % change
effect.applies_to: As above
effect.source: Kilmer et al. 2013

cost.unit: public cost per participant a year, near 0: participants pay $1 per test and up to $3 a day in South Dakota (twice-daily testing, about $730 to $1,095 a year paid by the participant); the sheriff's cost is about $0.10 a breath tube plus staff time
cost.source: South Dakota Attorney General fee schedule and program presentation, via search

fixes.sf_now: No 24/7 program in California; courts may order alcohol monitoring case by case [model knowledge — verify].

fixes.evidence_grade: moderate: one strong difference-in-differences study on arrests; no significant crash effect measured.

fixes.name: Sideshow and street-racing countermeasures: hardened intersections, roadside licence suspension and impound
fixes.how_it_works: Physical changes stop cars spinning in an intersection (raised dots, center islands, posts), and drivers caught racing or doing stunts lose their licence and car on the spot.

groups.mechanism: Extreme-speed and stunt driving is deterred by a certain, immediate penalty, and sideshow sites lose the open pavement that draws them.

effect.applies_to: Ontario's 2007 street racing and stunt driving law (roadside licence suspension and 7-day impound at 50 km/h over): interrupted time series found a sustained cut of about 58 speeding-related casualties a month among male drivers 16 to 24; the percent is not in the snippets read, so mid is a placeholder and should be filled from the paper [inference — mine]. No crash evaluation of hardened sideshow intersections was found

cost.unit: per intersection: not found; SF and Oakland sideshow hardening cost was not opened

fixes.name: Income-scaled (day) fines and graduated speeding penalties (Finland, Switzerland)
fixes.how_it_works: Fines for speeding are set as a number of days of the offender's income, so the penalty bites for every driver, and rise steeply with the speed over the limit.

groups.mechanism: A fine that is large for everyone deters repeat speeding by high-income drivers, whom flat fines barely touch.

fixes.name: Motorcycle ABS on every bike, and motorcyclist protective gear
fixes.how_it_works: Anti-lock brakes stop a motorcycle wheel locking in a hard stop, which is when riders fall; jackets, boots and gloves cut injury when they do.

groups.mechanism: Hard braking at speed is where a locked front wheel throws a rider; ABS keeps the bike upright.
groups.target_share: by_victim_role Other 217 hurt / 35 KSI of this group (size_families.families), likely mostly motorcyclists [inference — mine]

effect.unit: % change in motorcycle driver fatal crash involvements per registered vehicle year

groups.group: vehicles only | unsafe turn or lane use
groups.mechanism: Lane-change and turn conflicts often end in a rider braking hard; ABS shortens and stabilises the stop.

effect.applies_to: As above
